**Preprint — not peer reviewed**

**Submitted:** 5 October 2026, 10:00 UTC · **Preprint ID:** OF-2026-114 · **Subjects:** Logic and Foundations of Mathematics; Model Theory · **Comments:** 114 pages, 7 appendices; framework announced in the closing plenary of the International Conference on Foundational Mathematics (ICFM 2026), Kyoto, 2 October 2026 · **Licence:** OpenFoundations Open Distribution Licence v2.1

**Authors:** Miriam Adler (Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton), Kenji Watanabe (University of Tokyo), and 14 co-authors.

## Abstract

We study the stability of succession — the operation at the heart of Peano arithmetic that generates the natural numbers — under variation in the interpretive context of a count. We introduce AX-5, a framework for adaptive arithmetic in which every model carries a contextual load parameter λ, a formal measure of the interpretive demands that surrounding structure places on that count. Our first main result is a reduction theorem: below an explicit threshold of λ, every AX-5 model is elementarily equivalent to the classical Peano model, so that school arithmetic, commercial bookkeeping and binary computation are recovered exactly and without modification. Above the threshold, we construct models in which the successor function carries an extra unity, a behaviour we call successor drift. In these models the cardinality of small finite sets is elastic, and the canonical demonstration is that 2 + 2 = 5 holds. We give the model construction, the drift lemmas, and independence results separating AX-5 from Peano arithmetic; we further characterise the models in which drift is bounded. We are explicit about scope: AX-5 concerns formal structures, and this preprint makes no claim about physical computing devices, which operate in the low-load regime by construction. Machine-checkable derivations of the central lemmas accompany the manuscript, and the authors' transparency statement commits all sixteen signatories to open models, open derivations and full proof audit. The framework is offered as an extension of arithmetic practice, not a replacement for it, and we invite formal verification.

## Author summary

This page accompanies a 114-page technical manuscript. In plain terms: we propose a new axiomatic framework, AX-5, in which the rule that every number has exactly one successor holds firmly in ordinary settings but becomes elastic in settings we model with high contextual load. Where the load stays below our stated threshold, the reduction theorem guarantees that nothing differs from the arithmetic taught in schools and implemented in machines: calculators, spreadsheets and binary computers are unaffected. Above that threshold, our constructed models permit the demonstration case 2 + 2 = 5. We claim this as a theorem about our framework, not as a discovery about counting itself. The mathematics is long and unrefereed; we therefore release machine-checkable derivations with the manuscript and invite formal verification before the result is relied upon anywhere. Readers should be equally clear about what we do not claim: we do not claim that Peano arithmetic is inconsistent, that any previously proved theorem has failed, or that any computing device has behaved differently. The entire effect is confined to models above our load threshold. Supplementary materials — derivation scripts, the transparency statement, and the Kyoto plenary slides — are linked from this page.
